meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Buy land, they're not making it anymore'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Will Rogers. Quote Investigator traces this quip to an anonymous 1905 Kansas newspaper; the Rogers credit first appears in a 1954 real-estate ad.

answer.label: Not Will Rogers — an anonymous quip from 1905
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented in a Kansas newspaper, 13 October 1905 · creator unrecorded
answer.sourceLine: Nobody has produced a Will Rogers text containing this line. Quote Investigator ↗ found the earliest match in the McCracken Enterprise of McCracken, Kansas on 13 October 1905, where an unnamed “old gentleman” delivers it — the creator is anonymous. Rogers did write something adjacent in 1930, and the first credit to him is a 1954 real-estate advertisement.

source.heading: What the record shows

docMeta.dd: Will Rogers — and, just as often, Mark Twain
“God almighty isn’t making any more land, but he’s makin babies every mornin’”

source.excerpt: An old gentleman the other day in advising a friend to buy land, said, God almighty isn't making any more land, but he's makin babies every mornin'.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ found the earliest match in the McCracken Enterprise of McCracken, Kansas, 13 October 1905, spoken by an unnamed “old gentleman”; its timeline then tracks the joke through an “old Irishman” later in 1905, a Reverend C. L. Davis in 1916 and an unnamed clergyman in 1922 — all anonymous or non-famous speakers.

Independently, Barry Popik ↗ records a 1909 Salt Lake Telegram version — “ain’t nobody makin’ no more land” — and concludes that real-estate companies popularised the Will Rogers authorship in advertisements during the 1960s and 1970s.

What Rogers actually published is a different sentence. In a column dated 13 April 1930, quoted by Quote Investigator ↗, he wrote that he had put his money into ocean frontage “for the sole reason that there was only so much of it and no more, and that they wasent making any more.” Same logic, different subject, and twenty-five years after the joke was already circulating.

Wikiquote ↗ does list “Buy land. They ain’t making any more of the stuff” on its Rogers page, but under the heading “As quoted in …” and sourced only to Peter M. Wolf’s Land in America — a book catalogued as published in 1981 ↗. A second variant is marked “Unsourced.”
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest appearance Quote Investigator located, and the speaker is anonymous even here — an unnamed “old gentleman” quoted secondhand. A week later the same trail carries it as the saying of an unnamed “old Irishman.” The polished eight-word form the internet shares today has no identified author at all.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording has no identifiable author and no first-publication anchor — it is an anonymous American saying whose earliest documented ancestor is a 1905 Kansas newspaper paragraph, itself quoting an unnamed speaker. With no authored source work to date, no copyright status can responsibly be asserted for the line as it circulates today.

author.name: Will Rogers
author.heading: About Will Rogers
author.metaLine: 1879–1935 · American humorist, newspaper columnist & film actor
author.bio: Will Rogers was born on 4 November 1879 near Oologah in Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma, and died in a plane crash on 15 August 1935. A vaudeville rope-trick artist turned film star and “humorous social commentator,” he wrote a syndicated newspaper column from 1922 until his death and produced more than four thousand syndicated pieces — a body of homespun one-liners so large and so quotable that unattributed American folk wit tends to drift onto his name. This is one that drifted: the joke was in print while Rogers was still working the vaudeville circuit.

misattribution.heading: Two famous names, neither of them the source
misattribution.intro: America’s two most quotable humorists both get the credit for this one, and the record supports neither.

items.why: The quip was already in print in 1905, when Rogers was an unknown rope-trick performer. His nearest documented remark — a column of 13 April 1930 — is about ocean frontage, not land, and does not contain the phrase “buy land.” Quote Investigator ↗ dates the first credit to Rogers to a Miami Herald real-estate advertisement of 21 February 1954, years after his death in 1935.

Quote Investigator ↗ states it has found no substantive evidence that Twain, who died in 1910, ever used the quip; the Twain credit surfaces only in 1971. The line appears in no section of Wikiquote’s Mark Twain page ↗.

Wikiquote ↗ files the line under “As quoted in …” and cites only this book, whose catalogue record ↗ confirms a 1981 publication date. That is a modern secondary book repeating the attribution, not a text written by Rogers; Wikiquote marks a second variant simply “Unsourced.”

misattribution.truthLine: The real story: an anonymous American joke documented in a small Kansas newspaper on 13 October 1905 ↗, later handed to Will Rogers by real-estate advertising and to Mark Twain by 1971.

context.heading: Why it landed on Will Rogers
lead: The line is a real-estate salesman’s dream: a complete investment thesis in eight words, delivered as a joke. It needed a folksy American voice to carry it, and Will Rogers — cowboy, columnist, the humorist the whole country read — was the obvious fit. Barry Popik notes that real-estate companies popularised the Rogers authorship in advertisements ↗ through the 1960s and 1970s.

But the paper trail runs the other way. Quote Investigator’s timeline ↗ shows the gag passing through an anonymous “old gentleman” in 1905, an “old Irishman” a week later, a Reverend C. L. Davis in 1916 and an unnamed clergyman in 1922 — all before Rogers wrote a word on the subject. It is a folk joke that kept borrowing a speaker until it found one famous enough to stick.
detailsBody: What Rogers actually wrote, in a column dated 13 April 1930, was about ocean frontage rather than land: he had been putting his money into it “for the sole reason that there was only so much of it and no more, and that they wasent making any more.” It is the same reasoning, in his own spelling — but it is not the eight-word quip, and it arrived twenty-five years after the joke was already in print.

Mark Twain gets the credit at least as often. That attribution is later still: Quote Investigator ↗ dates it to 1971, when a London Evening Standard columnist wrote “Mark Twain said, ‘Buy land, they’ve stopped making it’” — and Twain had died in 1910. The quote does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s Mark Twain page ↗, in any section.
context.pull: A real-estate ad in 1954 handed the line to a man who had been dead since 1935.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator dates the earliest match to the McCracken Enterprise (McCracken, Kansas), 13 October 1905 — 'An old gentleman the other day in advising a friend to buy land, said, God almighty isn't making any more land, but he's makin babies every mornin'.' — and concludes the creator was anonymous, with no substantive evidence for Mark Twain and Rogers's related 1930 passage postdating the joke.

Quote Investigator reproduces Will Rogers's 13 April 1930 column passage ('I had been putting what little money I had in Ocean Frontage, for the sole reason that there was only so much of it and no more, and that they wasent making any more') and a Miami Herald K. M. Jones Real Estate advertisement of 21 February 1954 crediting Rogers with the concise quip.

Quote Investigator dates the first Mark Twain attributions to 1971 — a May 1971 London Evening Standard column ('Mark Twain said, "Buy land, they've stopped making it."') and a September 1971 Hammond, Indiana newspaper — and notes Twain died in 1910.

Barry Popik records a 23 February 1909 Salt Lake Telegram version ('ain't nobody makin' no more land'), notes the saying has been attributed to Will Rogers since the 1960s, and states that real-estate companies popularised the Will Rogers authorship in advertisements in the 1960s and 1970s.

Wikiquote's Will Rogers page lists 'Buy land. They ain't making any more of the stuff.' under the section heading 'As quoted in ...', sourced to Peter M. Wolf, Land in America: Its Value, Use, and Control (1981), p. 6, with the variant 'Buy land, they aren't making any more of it.' marked Unsourced.
Wikiquote's Mark Twain page does not contain this quote or any variant of it, in any section including Disputed and Misattributed.
Open Library catalogues 'Land in America: its value, use, and control' by Peter M. Wolf as published in 1981 (Pantheon Books, 1st edition, 590 pages).

Wikipedia states Will Rogers was born 4 November 1879 near Oologah in Indian Territory (Oklahoma) and died 15 August 1935; describes him as a vaudeville performer, actor and humorous social commentator; and records a syndicated weekly newspaper column running from 1922 to 1935 and more than 4,000 nationally syndicated columns.
